title: Operational Workload Simulator and Signature Guide
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview

This document describes the Operational Workload Simulator (OWS): a deterministic, configurable engine used by the eng-serving-runtime team to emulate customer traffic shapes, infer kernel-scheduler interactions, and produce telemetry signatures that feed the benchmarking and autotune pipelines. The OWS is intended for performance experiments, release validation, and as a canonical source of workload descriptors for replay across clouds and local sandboxes.

Goals

- Provide a small set (~8) of canonical workload signatures that cover >90% of production request shapes for text-generation and chat routes.
- Produce reproducible latency/cost buckets for CI and release verification.
- Emit annotated traces and kernel-hint suggestions to accelerate scheduling experiments.
- Be lightweight and portable: runnable in developer sandboxes and CI runners.

Workload signature taxonomy

Each signature is a compact descriptor summarizing the request distribution we want the runtime to see. Signatures are identified by id, human name, and a short rationale. Use the signature ids in experiments and report names.

Signature table (canonical set)

| id | name | request mix | mean tokens | percentile shape | primary risk | use case |
|----|------|-------------|-------------|------------------|--------------|----------|
| sig-llow | Low-latency chat (short-turn) | 90% chat-turn / 10% gen | 32 | tight (P99 ~ P95*1.2) | tail latency | UI chat, assistants |
| sig-lburst | Burst small prompts | 70% tiny / 30% small | 16 | spiky | scheduler warmstart | bot spiking behavior |
| sig-synth | Long generation seq | 100% generation | 1024 | heavy tail | memory pressure | document generation, summarization |
| sig-mix1 | Mixed enterprise | 50% chat / 30% embed / 20% gen | 128 | bi-modal | KV cache churn | multi-tenant enterprise |
| sig-embed | Embeddings heavy | 95% embed requests | 256 | narrow | throughput saturation | embedding pipelines |
| sig-prefetch | Stateful prefetched | 60% chat with KV hints | 64 | moderate | stale KV warmup | sessionized agents |
| sig-lowq | Low-quality cheap tokens | 100% short gen | 8 | narrow | over-batching | telemetry sampling |
| sig-noisy | Erratic unseen shapes | random mix | mixed | unpredictable | kernel thrash | chaos testing |

Simulator architecture (high level)

- Input: YAML workload descriptor (example below) describing arrival process, request templates, sequence lengths, and KV-cache locality.
- Orchestration: single binary (owsctl) schedules clients and records per-request metadata.
- Execution modes: local (single process), distributed (controller + worker), and CI-mode (deterministic RNG seeds).
- Outputs: time-series of latency percentiles, per-token cost estimate, kernel selection log, and full trace bundles (zip of trace.json + kernel-events.csv).

Workload descriptor (example YAML)

-- sample-workload.yaml --
name: long-document-summaries
id: sig-synth
seed: 20260201
arrival:
  distribution: poisson
  lambda: 0.8  # requests/sec per client
clients: 8
templates:
  - type: generation
    model_variants: ["rw-7b-q4f16", "rw-7b-fp16"]
    length:
      distribution: lognormal
      mu: 6.9  # exp(mu) ~ 1000 tokens
    temperature: 0.0
kv_locality: low
session_affinity: false
metrics_to_emit: [latency, kernel_hints, kv_miss_rate]

Kernel-hint mapping and guidance

The simulator emits a preliminary kernel_hint bundle that maps observed sequence-length histograms + concurrency to recommended kernel profile names. Use these hints to seed experimental scheduler policies or to annotate A/B runs. The guideline for interpreting hints is: 

- Hint level: "suggest" | "caution" | "avoid"
- Key signals used: mean_seq_len, tail_seq_len (P95/P99), kv_cache_hit_ratio, avg_concurrency, burst_index (max RPS / mean RPS)

Example kernel hint CSV (excerpt)

signature_id,mean_seq,P95_seq,kv_hit,avg_conc,burst_index,hint_level,recommended_profile
sig-synth,1024,2048,0.23,4,3.4,suggest,large-tile-qkv-fusion
sig-llow,32,48,0.88,16,1.3,avoid,large-batch-optimizations

Mapping rules (summary)

- If mean_seq > 512 and kv_hit < 0.4 -> prefer memory-efficient kernels, enable fragmented-kv-eviction.
- If avg_conc > 12 and burst_index < 2 -> enable continuous-batching aggressive slice.
- If burst_index > 3 and kv_hit > 0.7 -> warmstart fast-path kernels and prefetch KV.

Running experiments (step-by-step)

1. Prepare environment: export OWS_ARTIFACT_DIR=/tmp/ows-runs && mkdir -p $OWS_ARTIFACT_DIR
2. Pick signature YAML: examples/sig-llow.yaml
3. Run locally for quick smoke: ./owsctl run --profile local --config examples/sig-llow.yaml --out $OWS_ARTIFACT_DIR/sig-llow-20260218
4. For distributed: ./owsctl controller --config cluster-controller.yaml & then ./owsctl worker --join-controller http://controller:9000 --config examples/sig-synth.yaml
5. After run completes, generate report: ./owsctl report --input $OWS_ARTIFACT_DIR/sig-llow-20260218 --format html --output report-sig-llow.html

Repeatability and CI integration

- Use deterministic seeds in CI-mode; the runner will assert histogram equivalence (within tolerance) vs baseline.
- Baseline artifacts are stored in s3://redwood-bench-baselines/ows/ and referenced by signature id and git sha. CI job will fail on >5% regression in P99 latency for P50 traffic.

Telemetry emitted and acceptance criteria

Essential emitted signals:
- latency_p50/p95/p99 (ms)
- per_token_cost_estimate (USD/token)
- kernel_profile_distribution (counts)
- kv_cache_hit_rate
- gpu_utilization and mem_peak (MB)
- trace_bundle_url

Acceptance criteria for pre-release smoke (recommended):
- P50 change from baseline: < 2%
- P95 change from baseline: < 5%
- P99 change from baseline: < 10%
- Per-token cost delta: < 7% (absolute) or flagged for review
- Kernel-profile shift: no more than 2 suggested-profile changes for sig-llow and sig-embed

Experiment matrix and result naming

- Always include signature id + model variant + kernel-profile + run-seed in artifact names, e.g.: sig-synth__rw-7b-q4f16__large-tile-qkv-fusion__s20260201.zip
- Suggested matrix dimensions: signature x model_variant x concurrency x kernel_profile x quant_mode

Telemetry interpretation and correlation playbook (short)

1. Start with latency regressions: correlate P99 spikes with kernel_profile_distribution shifts and kv_cache_hit_rate drops.
2. If kernel events indicate repeated kernel load/unload, check burst_index and device memory fragmentation traces.
3. For throughput regressions, correlate GPU utilization vs avg_concurrency and queue_depth histograms.
4. For cost regressions, inspect per_token_cost_estimate and kernel time breakdown (attention vs decoder vs memcpy).

Troubleshooting checklist

- Symptom: Unexpected P99 increase in local runs
  1) Confirm deterministic seed and workload descriptor unchanged
  2) Check kernel_profile distribution in trace bundle; look for sudden "fallback" profile usage
  3) Inspect worker logs for OOMs / driver warnings
  4) Run with -v debug and attach sampling profiler: ./owsctl run --profile local --config X --debug-sampler

- Symptom: Different behavior in distributed vs local
  1) Verify clock skew and controller/worker time sync
  2) Confirm number of clients and threadpool sizes match (controller overrides matters)
  3) Check network latency histogram between controller and workers; high controller latency can artificially increase burst_index

Appendices

Appendix A — Common config flags
--threads N          # client threads per worker
--deterministic true # enable deterministic RNG
--emit-trace true    # create per-request trace bundles

Appendix B — Minimal example: quick local smoke
1) git checkout main && git pull origin main
2) ./owsctl run --profile local --config examples/sig-lowq.yaml --out /tmp/ows-quick
3) ./owsctl report --input /tmp/ows-quick --format text

Appendix C — Contact and escalation
- Slack: #eng-serving-runtime-bench (primary channel)
- Pager: eng-sre on-call for infra issues (see oncall roster)
- Pager escalation path: bench-owner -> runtime-sre -> infra-team

If you are adding a new workload signature, add a short rationale, expected badge (latency/cost vs baseline), and at least one representative production trace id in the related_pages field.
